title: Lineage: containment identities and verified parent crops
description: Inspect actual stored parent-child relationships, understand the display cap and distinguish a verified single-parent crop from the unsafe missing-child fallback.
objectives: Find Lineage inside Database Browser and build the real containment tree.
Distinguish complete counts, displayed families and typed object identities.
Recognize the incorrect family-crop fallback and inspect only a verified parent.
Use native crop zoom and distinguish the complete Python export from GUI controls.
prerequisite: Use the downloaded Annotate example with matching measurements and cell crops. The linked Graph Builder archive supplies the exact database but no images; the Lineage archive supplies the verified API CSV and review, not a replacement database. Do not use the current family-crop fallback to identify or label missing child images.

scenes.narration: Find Database Browser under Help, then open its nested Lineage tool. Here lineage means stored containment: which objects belong inside which cells. It is not a cell-division history, genetic ancestry or a new segmentation. The surrounding database controls belong to the host module.

Browse to measurements dot db from the real Annotate example and build the tree. This lesson uses an unchanged private copy. Widen the Object column and the divider if labels are cramped. Numeric labels repeat across fields and object types, so a number alone is not an identity.

The complete source contains two thousand three hundred forty-one cells, two thousand six hundred eighty-two nuclei and two thousand one hundred seventy-eight objects in the pathogen table. Only two thousand parent families appear in the tree; three hundred forty-one are omitted from display, not deleted from the database.

The summary says no cells have nothing inside, because a nucleus also counts as a child. That does not mean every cell contains a pathogen-table object: one thousand one hundred sixty-eight do not. No unattached children means every recorded parent exists, not that the segmentation is biologically correct.

Expand a parent to see its children. In this field, cell three contains nucleus five and pathogen one according to the stored links. These are typed object identities, not three interchangeable numbers. Selecting a child alone is different from selecting the whole family.

Select with contents publishes the parent and its children. Selecting the parent and a child together does not need a duplicate copy of that child. Published keys preserve field and object type, but the key column is hidden here. Publishing an identity does not prove that a matching crop exists.

Large families deserve inspection, not automatic biological interpretation. This example includes one family with thirty-three objects in total. Containment may reflect segmentation errors or other acquisition issues. The tree reports saved relationships; it does not validate unusual counts as a discovery.

Clicking a header sorts the displayed families without changing their containment. The two-thousand-parent display limit still applies. We checked every displayed identity and parent edge as well as the full hierarchy. Do not confuse a reordered or truncated view with an edited measurement table.

Open crops needs the Annotate screen, which supplies the image viewer. The actual message tells us to open Annotate first. A missing viewer is different from a missing image. Before requesting crops, load the matching example project in Annotate, not another run with coincidentally similar labels.

The downloaded project provides real cell crops. The database-only archive linked here cannot supply those images by itself. We use the complete matching example and preserve every original crop. Opening the source does not train a classifier or establish new labels.

There is a serious limitation in this build. Opening the three-object family displays cell three, then unrelated cell five and cell one crops instead of the requested nucleus and pathogen. The source has only cell crops. Reject this substitution: do not label those images as the missing children. This tutorial does not repair it.

The verified alternative is narrower: return to Lineage and double-click the parent cell alone. Unlike Open crops, this sends only that parent, not its family. Annotate now shows exactly the requested cell crop. We checked its identity and original image bytes; no child-crop support is implied.

Shift-click the parent thumbnail to enlarge its existing preview without assigning a class. Escape returns to the grid. This helps visual inspection but creates no extra image resolution. Use the correct gesture: an ordinary left click is an annotation action, not the zoom demonstrated here.

Build tree refreshes the containment view. For Python, read_object_tables, build_forest and lineage_frame expose the same structure. The linked CSV contains all seven thousand two hundred one nodes, including families omitted from display. It was written by the API, not a Lineage export button, and is not biological validation.
